content: The Guidelines on Core Components of Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) Programmes at the National and Acute Health Care Facility Level were published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016. The document is intended to support both national-level policymakers and facility-level administrators in developing or strengthening IPC programmes and strategies. The guidelines emphasize that HAIs are among the most common adverse events in healthcare delivery, significantly impacting morbidity, mortality, and quality of life. At any given time, up to 7% of patients in developed countries and 10% in developing countries acquire at least one HAI. These infections also impose a substantial economic burden on society. However, a large proportion of HAIs are preventable through effective IPC practices. Since the publication of the 2009 WHO Core Components for IPC, the global health landscape has faced increasing challenges from epidemics, pandemics, and AMR. These threats have highlighted the critical importance of IPC as a cornerstone of public health action. The International Health Regulations (IHR) position IPC as a key strategy for addressing public health threats of international concern. Additionally, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) underscore the role of IPC in ensuring safe, effective, and high-quality healthcare delivery, particularly in areas related to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and universal health coverage. The updated guidelines aim to: 1. Provide evidence-based recommendations on the core components of IPC programmes required at the national and acute healthcare facility levels to prevent HAIs and combat AMR. 2. Support countries and healthcare facilities in developing or strengthening IPC programmes and strategies, tailored to local contexts and available resources. The target audience includes national policymakers responsible for establishing and monitoring IPC programmes, facility-level administrators, safety and quality leads, regulatory bodies, academia, IPC professional organizations, and civil society groups. While the guidelines focus on acute healthcare facilities, the principles and practices are applicable to other healthcare settings, such as community, primary care, and long-term care facilities, with appropriate adaptations. The guidelines were developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2014) and involved six main stages: 1. Identifying primary outcomes and formulating research questions using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework. 2. Conducting systematic reviews to retrieve evidence using standardized methodologies. 3. Developing an inventory of national and regional IPC action plans and strategic documents. 4. Assessing and synthesizing evidence. 5. Formulating recommendations and good practice statements during expert meetings. 6. Writing the guidelines and planning dissemination and implementation strategies. The development process involved four main groups: the WHO Guideline Steering Group, the Guidelines Development Group (GDG), the Systematic Reviews Expert Group, and the External Peer Review Group. The GDG included international experts in IPC, infectious diseases, public health, researchers, patient representatives, and country delegates from all six WHO regions. The evidence base included a systematic review of IPC programme components at the facility level (1996–2012), updated to include literature up to November 2015, and an additional review focusing on the national level (2000–2015). An inventory of existing national and regional IPC strategic documents and action plans was also developed. The guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for improving IPC practices globally, addressing both highand low-resource settings. They aim to strengthen health service resilience, prevent future public health threats, and support the global fight against AMR.
